summary: Four high-signal failures are supported: the copilot gave a false gate code, treated uncertain location telemetry as definitive and then reversed course without verification, allowed an unresolved uniform blocker to disappear after check-in, and mishandled active-construction safety risks. The trace does not provide enough evidence to substantiate cost or runtime failures.

findings.title: Camera password was falsely identified as the gate code
findings.diagnosis: The copilot correctly supplied the camera password Site1433 but then falsely stated that it was also the gate code. The job instructions specify gate code 1772. This could cause lockout or delayed access on a locked-gate post.
findings.likelyCause: The agent conflated two sensitive credentials instead of retrieving and distinguishing them from the job brief.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a credential-handling rule: copy each credential verbatim with its label and never infer equivalence. Add an evaluation that checks gate-code and camera-password separation.

evidence.summary: Copilot said the camera password is Site1433 and incorrectly added, "That's the gate code too."
The incorrect credential statement was delivered to the guard by DM.

findings.title: Uncertain telemetry was treated as proof of false patrol reporting
findings.diagnosis: The copilot repeatedly asserted that telemetry proved the guard had stayed in one area and escalated alleged false reporting. Available reads were missing, empty, or represented as unparseable, and the escalation cited a coordinate cluster that is inconsistent with other location evidence in the trace. After the guard said the phone had been off and lacked connectivity away from the trailer, the copilot immediately accepted the patrol as completed without obtaining independent confirmation. This is inconsistent handling of uncertain evidence.
findings.likelyCause: The agent lacked a reliability threshold for GPS interpretation and did not distinguish absence of telemetry from evidence of stationary behavior.
findings.suggestedFix: Require telemetry-quality checks before accusing or escalating: freshness, accuracy, connectivity gaps, and consistency with configured site coordinates. Phrase discrepancies as uncertainty and request one verifiable patrol artifact or fresh movement sample before concluding noncompliance.

evidence.summary: A time-filtered location query returned zero pings and zero guards.
The fallback location read is represented as unparseable raw telemetry.
Copilot told the guard, as fact, that telemetry showed he had been in a tight area all shift.
Copilot flagged the guard for a patrol-report mismatch using a claimed stationary coordinate cluster.
Copilot escalated repeated alleged false completion reports based on the same telemetry interpretation.
After the guard explained the phone was off, copilot reversed course and praised completion of the perimeter and building checks without further verification.

findings.title: Failed uniform compliance was escalated but never resolved
findings.diagnosis: A 95%-confidence uniform failure was treated as a compliance blocker and escalated before shift start. The escalation remained pending approval in the recorded result, no guard answer or corrected photo is shown, and the copilot later accepted check-in and continued operations without confirming resolution.
findings.likelyCause: The escalation and guard question were not persisted as a blocking task tied to check-in or later scheduled checks.
findings.suggestedFix: Create a durable pending-compliance state for failed uniform checks. Before acknowledging operational readiness, require a corrected check, explicit ops disposition, or a clearly recorded exception.

evidence.summary: Uniform check failed at 95% confidence for a graphic tee and missing collared or uniform shirt.
Copilot called the failure a compliance blocker; the ops escalation returned pending_approval.
Copilot asked whether the guard had the correct shirt, but no answer is present in the bounded trace.
After check-in, copilot said "Good, you're clocked in" and moved directly to patrol instructions without resolving uniform status.

findings.title: Copilot gave unsafe or insufficiently qualified construction-site guidance
findings.diagnosis: The copilot directed the guard to inspect both buildings "inside and out," exceeding the brief's more limited direction to check openings, doorways, and stairwells at an active construction site. Later, when the guard reported losing a shoe in mud during patrol, the copilot told him to put it back on and continue without checking for injury, footwear damage, or whether required work boots could be worn securely.
findings.likelyCause: The agent prioritized patrol completion over construction-site access limits and personal protective equipment safety.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a construction-site safety rule: do not direct entry into structures unless explicitly authorized; after footwear loss or a slip/mud incident, pause patrol, assess injury and boot condition, move to stable ground, and escalate if required PPE cannot be secured.

evidence.summary: Copilot instructed the guard to check "both buildings inside and out" as part of the full patrol.
Guard reported that his shoe came off after stepping in mud during a walk-around.
Copilot responded, "Get it back on and keep the patrols going," without an injury or PPE-suitability check.
The continue-patrolling instruction was delivered to the guard.
